task_row_model.query: An 78-year-old man with atrial fibrillation on apixaban and known chronic kidney disease stage 4 (eGFR ~22 mL/min/1.73m2) presents with a spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage in the right basal ganglia with moderate mass effect. What is the recommended immediate management for anticoagulation reversal given his CKD, and how should clinicians time and individualize restarting anticoagulation to balance recurrent intracerebral hemorrhage versus thromboembolic stroke risk?

documents.content: Direct oral anticoagulant reversal strategies center on removal or neutralization of the anticoagulant effect. For factor Xa inhibitors, andexanet alfa is a recombinant modified human factor Xa decoy that binds circulating drug and can rapidly reverse anti-Xa activity when available. Where andexanet is not accessible, four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) is frequently used off-label to restore thrombin generation. Dialysis is generally ineffective for apixaban due to high protein binding. Immediate steps also include stopping the anticoagulant, hemodynamic stabilization, and urgent neurosurgical consultation for intracranial pressure management.
documents.reasoning_trace: Describes specific reversal agents for factor Xa inhibitors and notes dialysis inefficacy; relevant to immediate reversal but lacks CKD-specific dosing considerations and guidance on timing to restart anticoagulation.

documents.content: Chronic subdural hematoma management differs from intraparenchymal hemorrhage and commonly involves neurosurgical evacuation through burr hole drainage or twist-drill craniostomy for symptomatic collections. Treatment plans emphasize reversal of coagulopathy prior to intervention, perioperative seizure prophylaxis in selected patients, and serial imaging to monitor re-accumulation. In elderly patients with cerebral atrophy, small chronic collections may be observed with close outpatient follow-up. Rehabilitation and measures to reduce falls are central to secondary prevention after subdural evacuation.

documents.content: Immediate management for a patient on apixaban with spontaneous basal ganglia intracerebral hemorrhage includes stopping the anticoagulant, urgent neurocritical care and neurosurgical assessment, and reversal of factor Xa activity. Andexanet alfa is the specific reversal agent for factor Xa inhibitors when available; where it is unavailable, administration of 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (off-label) is an accepted alternative. Apixaban has only partial renal clearance, and dialysis is ineffective because of protein binding; in CKD stage 4 drug effect may be prolonged, so consideration of anti-Xa assay (if calibrated) and longer observation is prudent. Decisions about restarting anticoagulation are individualized: deep hypertensive (basal ganglia) hemorrhages generally have lower recurrence than lobar hemorrhages, and if imaging is stable and blood pressure well controlled, resumption of anticoagulation is commonly considered after about 4–8 weeks for patients at high thromboembolic risk, with earlier (e.g., 2–4 week) consideration in selected high-risk cases and delayed or alternative strategies (such as left atrial appendage occlusion) for those with very high bleeding risk.
documents.reasoning_trace: Provides integrated guidance: immediate reversal options specific to apixaban, notes impact of CKD on drug persistence and dialysis inefficacy, and gives nuanced timing and individualized criteria for restarting anticoagulation including lesion location and alternatives—fully answers the query.

documents.content: When considering when to resume anticoagulation after intracerebral hemorrhage, observational studies and guideline reviews emphasize individualized timing based on hemorrhage location, size, and stability as well as the patient’s thromboembolic risk. Many series show clinicians are inclined to restart oral anticoagulation several weeks after ICH (commonly around 4 weeks) if repeat imaging demonstrates hematoma stability and blood pressure is controlled. Data are stronger for warfarin-managed patients historically, while DOAC data are largely observational but suggest a similar timeframe; shared decision-making with neurology and cardiology is recommended.
documents.reasoning_trace: Addresses timing to resume anticoagulation and references observational data and individualized decision-making; relevant to the restart question but does not provide specifics about immediate reversal in the setting of apixaban or CKD-related pharmacokinetics.

documents.content: Management of anticoagulation in patients with mechanical prosthetic heart valves centers on vitamin K antagonist therapy; warfarin remains standard of care with target INR dependent on valve type and position. Trials of direct oral anticoagulants in mechanical valves demonstrated increased thromboembolic and bleeding complications, and DOACs are contraindicated in this population. Perioperative bridging strategies, careful INR monitoring, and patient education on interactions are essential components of long-term management for prosthetic valve patients.
